The statute sets no day count and no money penalty. The point that a bare code is not a specific reason comes from 29 CFR 2590.715-2719(b)(2)(ii)(E)(3) (code plus its meaning plus the plan's standard), which binds only non-grandfathered group health plans.

This period may be extended one time by the plan for up to 15 days, provided that the plan administrator both determines that such an extension is necessary due to matters beyond the control of the plan and notifies the claimant, prior to the expiration of the initial 30-day period, of the circumstances requiring the extension of time and the date by which the plan expects to render a decision. FAQ A-10: "While the regulation establishes time frames within which claims must be decided, the regulation does not address the periods within which payments that have been granted must be actually paid or services that have been approved must be actually rendered. checks.correction: Citation, 30 days, one 15-day extension, the 45-day response window and the (f)(4) start-at-filing and tolling rules are right (eCFR text current as of 2026-11-19). Two fixes. (1) The extension is valid only if the plan 'determines that such an extension is necessary due to matters beyond the control of the plan' AND sends the notice before day 30; the researcher dropped the first condition, which is itself a lever (a backlog is within the plan's control). (2) The deadline is for the decision notice, not for payment (FAQ A-10). Silence with no payment is a missed notice of an adverse benefit determination (a failure to pay is one under (m)(4)), but a claim the plan approved and is holding for the employer to fund (UMR UM1491: 'The customer chooses which day of the week/month to release payment.') is a fiduciary payment-timing issue under ERISA Part 4, not a missed decision deadline. 45 CFR 147.136(b)(3)(i) applies the same rule to individual-market (exchange) issuers 'as if the issuer were a group health plan'. Consequence: see E09 for the circuit caveat.

checks.quote: (F)(1): "In the case of a plan or issuer that fails to strictly adhere to all the requirements of this paragraph (b)(2) with respect to a claim, the claimant is deemed to have exhausted the internal claims and appeals process of this paragraph (b) ... checks.correction: Regulatory text verified verbatim. Three fixes to the stated effect. (1) Deemed exhaustion opens external review only for claims inside 2719(d)(1) (medical judgment, No Surprises Act, rescission); for coding, bundling or rate denials it opens only the door to court. (2) The court effect depends on the circuit. Kentucky (6th Cir.): Daniel (1988) holds a deemed denial does not change the standard of review, and the E.D. For the open 422.520 question, its text: (a)(1) 95 percent of clean claims within 30 days for services 'not furnished under a written agreement', (a)(2) interest on late clean claims, (a)(3) 'All other claims from non-contracted providers must be paid or denied within 60 calendar days from the date of the request.' Whether it binds the HCPP through 422.568(c) remains unconfirmed with CMS.

checks.citation: 29 CFR 2590.716-3 (health care facility; visit); 29 CFR 2590.716-5(b), (c)(3)-(4); 45 CFR 149.420(b)(1)(i); CMS/DOL/Treasury ACA-CAA FAQs Part 55, Q16-Q17 and footnote 34 (Aug. 19, 2022)
checks.quote: 716-5(c)(3): "Not later than 30 calendar days after the bill for the items or services is transmitted by the provider ... must determine whether the items and services are covered under the plan or coverage and, if the items and services are covered, send to the provider an initial payment or a notice of denial of payment. For purposes of this paragraph (c)(3), the 30-calendar-day period begins on the date the plan or issuer receives the information necessary to decide a claim for payment for the items or services." 149.420(b)(1)(i): "Items and services related to emergency medicine, anesthesiology, pathology, radiology, and neonatology, whether provided by a physician or non-physician practitioner;"
checks.correction: Verified, including the facility list (hospital, hospital outpatient department, critical access hospital, ASC) and FAQ Q16-Q17 (complaints: No Surprises Help Desk 1-800-985-3059). Additions: FAQ footnote 34 says a plan 'does not satisfy its obligation' if it sends the initial payment or denial to the patient instead of the provider; 716-3 defines 'visit' to include 'laboratory services ... regardless of whether the provider furnishing such items or services is at the facility', which brings pathology reads of specimens from an in-network facility visit into scope. Retiree-only ERISA plans are exempt (29 U.S.C. 1191a(a)).

checks.quote: 149.510(d)(1)(iii): "After making a payment determination, the certified IDR entity will retain the certified IDR entity fee described under paragraph (d)(1)(i) of this section paid by the non-prevailing party ... The certified IDR entity must return the fee paid by the prevailing party ... within 30 business days following the date of the certified IDR entity's payment determination." 716-6(d)(1)(ii): "(A) A statement that the service code or modifier billed by the provider, facility, or provider of air ambulance services was downcoded; (B) An explanation of why the claim was downcoded, which must include a description of which service codes were altered, if any, and a description of which modifiers were altered, added, or removed, if any; and (C) The amount that would have been the qualifying payment amount had the service code or modifier not been downcoded;"
checks.correction: Deadlines, fee ranges ($200-$840 single, $268-$1,173 batched, $75-$250 per extra 25 lines), the $15 administrative fee for disputes from June 11, 2026 and the FR citations are verified. Fixes: (1) 'the losing party keeps the IDR entity fee' is wrong wording: the IDR entity keeps the non-prevailing party's fee and refunds the prevailing party's fee within 30 business days. (2) The 50-item batch cap is in the amended (c)(4)(i), which (h)(4) applies only to disputes whose open negotiation begins 90 days after the Departments announce the new functionality; until then (h)(10) keeps the pre-June 4, 2026 rule, whose batching test is same NPI or TIN, same plan, same or similar service code, furnished within the same 30-business-day period, with no 50-item cap. Additions: 716-6(d)(1)(v) requires, 'For disclosures required to be provided on or after August 3, 2026, the legal business name (if any) of the self-insured group health plan or issuer and, if applicable, the legal business name of the self-insured group health plan sponsor, and the registration number', which names the sponsor without a Form 5500 search; (d)(1)(iv)(A)(2) adds notice to the Secretary through the IDR portal once available.

checks.citation: UMR provider FAQ UM1491 (0924); Cigna Appeals and Disputes Policy and Procedures page; UnitedHealthcare 'Pre- and post-service appeals and reconsiderations' page; 2026 UnitedHealthcare Care Provider Administrative Guide (Commercial, Individual Exchange, Medicare Advantage), Chapter 10
checks.quote: UHC page: "Timing: You have 12 months to complete the following steps: Step 1: File a claim reconsideration request. Step 2: File an appeal if you disagree with the outcome of the claim reconsideration decision." UHC guide: "You must submit your reconsideration and appeal to us within 12 months from the date of the original claim EOB or PRA (or as required by law or your Agreement)." Cigna: "Submit the appeal within 180 calendar days of the date of the initial payment or denial notice" ... "Customers cannot be billed for any amount denied because you failed to submit the request for review or arbitration within the required timelines."
checks.correction: UMR and Cigna quotes verified. Fixes and additions: (1) UHC does state a number: 12 months for reconsideration plus appeal together (page and 2026 guide), not only 'per participation agreement'. (2) UHC: 'Most network health care professionals ... that provide services to UnitedHealthcare Medicare Advantage (including D-SNP), UnitedHealthcare Community Plan (Medicaid) and commercial plan members are required to submit reconsiderations and pre- and post-service appeals digitally', so faxing UHC network appeals is the wrong channel. (3) UHC guide: an overpayment or recoupment disagreement is due 'within 30 calendar days ... from the date of receipt of notification'; a Notice of Dispute is due 'no later than 60 days after the date of our decision on your appeal' unless the Agreement differs, and 'Failure to timely comply ... will result in the waiver of your right to initiate dispute resolution and waiver of your right to pursue such claim or issue in any forum.' (4) UHC bulk route: 20 or more paid or denied claims with the same administrative issue go in one Claims Research Project online. (5) Cigna: a missed 180-day window makes 'the last Cigna Healthcare determination' final and the patient cannot be billed, so the dollars are lost outright; review 'completed in 60 days' with notice 'within 75 business days'; appeals to Cigna National Appeals Unit, PO Box 188011, Chattanooga, TN 37422 (PO Box 188062 for GWH-Cigna or 'G' cards); no medical-appeal fax is published. (6) UMR: 'At UMR, claims are denied for additional information (not pended)', and UHSS 'is neither an insurance company nor a TPA'.

missing: DOL Claims Procedure FAQ A-10 (dol.gov FAQ page, verified via Internet Archive copy of 2026-11-05): the claims deadlines do not govern payment, but 'Failure to provide services or benefit payments within reasonable periods of time following plan approval, however, may present fiduciary responsibility issues under Part 4 of title I of ERISA.' This is the lever for UMR-style claims that are processed but not funded until the employer releases payment.

DOL Claims Procedure FAQ B-5 (same page): relevant documents under 29 CFR 2560.503-1(m)(8)(iii) can include 'the specific plan rules or guidelines governing the application of specific protocols, criteria, rate tables, fee schedules, etc. to claims like the claim at issue'. Ask for the fee schedule or pricing table behind every out-of-network underpayment.

DOL Claims Procedure FAQs D-9 and D-10: the plan 'must provide the identity of any such experts when requested by a claimant', and 'merely providing the name of the company employing the expert or the qualifications of the expert would not ... satisfy' 29 CFR 2560.503-1(h)(3)(iv). This is the strongest verified lever against vendor or automated reviews.

DOL Claims Procedure FAQ C-16: a notice that 'merely indicates ... that a rule, guideline, protocol, or similar criterion may have been relied upon' does not meet 29 CFR 2560.503-1(g)(1)(v)(A); FAQ C-12: any payment below the billed amount is an adverse benefit determination requiring a compliant notice.

DOL Claims Procedure FAQ F-2: for plans governed only by 29 CFR 2560.503-1(l)(1) (grandfathered and retiree-only plans), the claimant bears 'the burden of proving' a procedural failure, and an inadvertent omission such as the plan provision may be curable, while 'systematic deviations' or a notice missing the review procedures justify court. Use it to set the tone of letters to those plans.

DOL Claims Procedure FAQ B-3: when the patient 'clearly designates an authorized representative to act and receive notices', the plan 'should ... direct all information and notifications' to the representative. Getting the notices is what starts the practice's own clocks.

29 CFR 2560.503-1(f)(2)(iii)(B): a 15-day extension is allowed only if 'necessary due to matters beyond the control of the plan' and noticed before day 30; an extension letter citing volume or routine review is challengeable (eCFR, current to 2026-11-19).

Fessenden v. Reliance Standard Life Ins. Co., No. 18-1346 (7th Cir. June 25, 2019) (appeal from N.D. Ind.; court PDF at https://cases.justia.com/federal/appellate-courts/ca7/18-1346/18-1346-2019-06-25.pdf): 'When a plan administrator commits a procedural violation, however, it loses the benefit of deference and a de novo standard applies' and 'the "substantial compliance" exception does not apply to blown deadlines.' Binding in Indiana; a real consequence for a missed ERISA deadline.

Kentucky caution: Daniel v. Eaton Corp., 839 F.2d 263, 267 (6th Cir. 1988) ('the standard of review is no different whether the appeal is actually denied or is deemed denied'), applied as still binding by Van Winkle v. Life Ins. Co. of N. Am., No. 12-253-KSF (E.D. Ky. May 8, 2013). In the Sixth Circuit, do not promise that a missed deadline brings de novo review; cite 2719(b)(2)(ii)(F)(1)'s own words for non-grandfathered plans.

Brown v. BlueCross BlueShield of Tenn., No. 15-5739 (6th Cir. 2016), Part II: 'a healthcare provider does not qualify as a statutory beneficiary under ERISA' (no standing of its own), citing Pa. Chiropractic Ass'n v. Independence Hosp. Indem. Plan, 802 F.3d 926, 930 (7th Cir. 2015) for the Seventh Circuit. Suit rights exist only through a valid assignment.

29 CFR 2590.715-2719(d)(1)(i)(A): whether a denial involves medical judgment is 'determined by the external reviewer', so the plan cannot screen out medical-necessity, level-of-care or modifier-necessity denials from federal external review by calling them administrative.

29 CFR 2590.716-6(d)(1)(v) (added 91 FR 34059, June 4, 2026): for No Surprises Act disclosures due on or after August 3, 2026 the plan must state 'the legal business name (if any) of the self-insured group health plan or issuer and, if applicable, the legal business name of the self-insured group health plan sponsor, and the registration number'; and FAQs Part 55 footnote 34: an initial payment or denial sent to the patient instead of the provider does not satisfy the 30-day rule.

UnitedHealthcare 2026 Care Provider Administrative Guide, Chapter 10 (https://www.uhcprovider.com/content/dam/provider/docs/public/admin-guides/2026-UHC-Administrative-Guide.pdf) and the UHC appeals page: 12 months total from the original EOB or PRA for reconsideration and appeal; 30 calendar days to dispute an overpayment or recoupment notice; Notice of Dispute within 60 days after the appeal decision or the claim is waived 'in any forum'; digital submission required for network providers; 20 or more same-issue claims can go in one Claims Research Project. These are hard contract deadlines RemitWatch must calendar.

UnitedHealthcare 2026 Administrative Guide, 'Capitation and/or delegation supplement', heading 'ERISA claims processing': UHC tells its delegated claim payers 'you must issue denials within 30 calendar days of receipt of the complete claim. You must issue payments within 30 calendar days or within state regulation, whichever is more stringent' and 'Interest must be automatically paid on all uncontested claims not paid within 30-calendar-days after receipt of the claim.' This is UHC's own published standard for its delegates, not federal law (ERISA has no payment deadline, FAQ A-10); quote it to UHC only as its own stated practice.

Cigna Appeals and Disputes page: if the provider misses the 180-day appeal or the one-year arbitration request, 'the last Cigna Healthcare determination will be final. Customers cannot be billed for any amount denied because you failed to submit the request for review or arbitration within the required timelines.' The appeal-path table routes bundling, mutually exclusive and modifier denials to the provider appeal, benefit and maximum-reimbursable-amount denials to the customer appeal, and medical necessity to either.

26 U.S.C. 4980D(f)(3) and (b)(3): a failure counts as corrected only if 'retroactively undone to the extent possible' and the person is placed 'in a financial position which is as good as such person would have been in had such failure not occurred'; for failures not corrected before an IRS examination notice the tax per individual is at least the lesser of $2,500 (or $15,000 if more than de minimis) or the tax figured without the reasonable-diligence and 30-day-correction limits (4980D(b)(3)). Treasury's parallel claims rule is 26 CFR 54.9815-2719.

26 U.S.C. 9712(b) and 9702(a)(2): the UMWA 1992 Plan and Combined Fund cover retirees and their dependents only, so under 29 U.S.C. 1191a(a) and 26 U.S.C. 9831(a)(2) the ACA claims additions, federal external review, the No Surprises Act and the 4980D excise tax very likely do not reach them; only 29 CFR 2560.503-1 does.

42 U.S.C. 300gg-22(a)(2) and (b)(1): HHS civil money penalties reach issuers only where HHS finds the state 'has failed to substantially enforce' the provision; HHS enforces directly against non-federal governmental plans. For insured Kentucky and Indiana plans the regulator to name is the state insurance department.
